reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / movement disorder literature
clinicalPearls: Sudden jerks producing flexion (or occasionally extension) of the trunk, neck and hips, arising from a generator in the spinal cord
Jerks characteristically appear or worsen during relaxed wakefulness and the transition to sleep, often when lying down
The movements spread slowly up and down the cord from a thoracic or abdominal origin, reflecting conduction along propriospinal pathways
Neurophysiology can demonstrate the slow rostro-caudal propagation and a consistent muscle recruitment pattern
A substantial proportion of clinically diagnosed cases are ultimately shown to be functional
Back-averaging and the presence of a Bereitschaftspotential help distinguish organic from functional cases
reference.pathophysiology: Propriospinal myoclonus is generated within the spinal cord, with an initial focus in the mid-thoracic region from which activity propagates slowly up and down the cord along propriospinal interneuronal pathways, producing axial jerks. In some patients a structural spinal lesion is found, but many have no identifiable lesion and a significant number are demonstrated to be functional, in which a premovement Bereitschaftspotential and variable, distractible features indicate a voluntary-type mechanism experienced as involuntary.
additionalInvestigations: Surface electromyography with polygraphy to show slow propagation and recruitment pattern
Back-averaging to seek a premovement Bereitschaftspotential (suggesting functional origin)
MRI of the spinal cord to exclude a structural lesion
Assessment for functional signs such as variability and distractibility
Sleep study if the relationship to sleep onset is prominent
redFlags: A structural spinal cord lesion on imaging
Associated sensory level, weakness or sphincter disturbance
Features suggesting a broader neurological disorder
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with cause; lesional cases depend on the underlying pathology, while functional cases can improve with appropriate explanation and therapy, though the disorder is often persistent.
pitfalls: Assuming an organic spinal cause without seeking a Bereitschaftspotential
Missing a structural spinal lesion in genuinely lesional cases
Confusing it with benign hypnic jerks
Not recognising the high proportion of functional cases
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Image the spinal cord and treat any identified structural lesion driving the axial jerks
For symptomatic organic myoclonus, trial pharmacotherapy such as clonazepam, with levetiracetam or zonisamide as alternatives
When investigation indicates a functional disorder, deliver a clear, positive explanation of the diagnosis as the basis of treatment
Treat functional cases with tailored physiotherapy and cognitive behavioural therapy rather than escalating drug therapy
Address the sleep-onset relationship with sleep hygiene advice and reassurance
Manage through a multidisciplinary team including neurology, physiotherapy and neuropsychiatry or clinical psychology
